cases.question_text:

This case is a middle-aged female with a breast mass.
choices_raw: D. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma
cases.histology: This case depicts breast tissue with mixed acute, chronic, and granulomatous inflammation surrounding lobules and spanning larger portions of the breast biopsy cores. There are variably sized cystic spaces within the granulomatous inflammation. On high power inspection, the cystic spaces are rimmed with neutrophils.
cases.discussion: Cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis (CNGM) is a rare subtype of mastitis that is often associated with Corynebacterium infection, though this can be challenging to prove histologically. CNGM consists of granulomas or lipogranulomas with mixed inflammation, often centered around lobules within the breast. Lesions are typically unilateral and the majority present as a mass. Corynebacterium are gram positive bacilli and can be visible on gram stain (e.g., Gram-Weigert) within the cystic spaces. While cystic spaces are characteristic, and they are not strictly necessary for diagnosis. When granulomatous inflammation is present in the breast, mycobacterial or fungal infections should be considered. It is also important to rule out breast carcinomas, especially in older patients, as they can rarely have a granulomatous inflammatory reaction. If the patient has had previous surgical procedure in the breast, granulomatous inflammation can also result from a foreign body giant cell reaction to foreign materials.

references.text: Wu JM, Turashvili G. Cystic neutrophilic granulomatous mastitis: an update. J Clin Pathol. 2020 Aug;73(8):445-453. doi: 10.1136/jclinpath-2019-206180. Epub 2020 Feb 24. PMID: 32094275.

cases.title: Week 776: Case 1
cases.attribution: Cases presented by Dr. Ashley Cimino-Mathews and prepared by Dr. Katherine Fomchenko.
cases.vignette: This case is a young female with a nipple mass.
cases.question_text:
Cases presented by Dr. Ashley Cimino-Mathews and prepared by Dr. Katherine Fomchenko.
This case is a young female with a nipple mass.
cases.histology: Examination of the breast tissue reveals an infiltrative lesion comprised of epithelioid cells with round nuclei, centrally located and prominent nucleoli, and abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm. The cells are infiltrating around and through benign ducts and lobules with no evidence of an atypical intraductal proliferation. There is minimal appreciable mitotic activity. Though not shown in this case, immunostains would show the cells to be diffusely immunoreactive for S100 and inhibin, and to be negative for AE1/AE3 and Cam5.2.
cases.discussion: This case depicts a granular cell tumor, which is a rare type of peripheral nerve sheath tumor arising from Schwann cells that can infrequently involve the breast. Granular cell tumors characteristically involve the head and neck and skin, where they can incite a prominent pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia in overlying squamous epithelium. In the breast, granular cell tumors clinically, radiographically and grossly mimic infiltrating carcinoma because they can appear as a fixed, stellate, and infiltrative solid mass. They may occur sporadically or in the setting of prior surgery. Histologically, granular cell tumors display abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm and can be either epithelioid or spindled, and occur either as nests of cells or as single-file rows of cells. The case illustrated here does exhibit atypical features including prominent nucleoli, but does not meet criteria for malignancy. The differential diagnosis includes histiocytic proliferations such as xanthogranulomatous inflammation and fat necrosis, as well as other pink cell tumors—melanoma, apocrine carcinomas, and histiocytoid lobular carcinomas. Immunohistochemistry can resolve any diagnostic dilemma, as granular cell tumors are immunoreactive for inhibin, CD68, S100 protein, and NSE, and are negative for cytokeratin and more specific melanocytic markers (HMB45, Melan A). Most granular cell tumors are benign and are adequately treated with complete surgical excision.

cases.vignette: This case is an elderly male who underwent a partial scrotum resection.
cases.question_text:
Cases presented by Dr. Ezra Baraban and prepared by Dr. Katherine Fomchenko.
This case is an elderly male who underwent a partial scrotum resection.
choices_raw: B. Pagetoid spread of urothelial carcinoma
cases.feedback_text: Sections show skin with an intraepithelial population of neoplastic cells with ample cytoplasm with focal duct or gland formation. Melanoma in-situ could be considered, but in areas the tumor cells form clusters and glands with intracytoplasmic mucin, indicating glandular differentiation. Lack of SOX10 or Melan-A expression also excludes melanoma. Squamous cell carcinoma in-situ could show pagetoid growth, but tumor cells should label with squamous markers such as high molecular weight keratin and/or P63/40. A population of cytologically malignant glandular epithelial cells colonizing benign squamous epithelium is diagnostic of Paget’s disease. These cells often have an adnexal immunophenotype and can have an immunoprofile quite similar to breast carcinoma, including labeling with GATA3, GCDFP15, and/or mammaglobin in addition to ER/PR and/or HER2. On the basis of morphology alone, it is very difficult to distinguish from extension from an underlying visceral primary such as colon or bladder, therefore clinical evaluation for an underlying invasive or in-situ neoplasm is mandatory.

cases.source_answer: D. Prostate adenocarcinoma, Grade Group 5, with pleomorphic giant cell features
cases.correct_answer: Prostate adenocarcinoma, Grade Group 5, with pleomorphic giant cell features
cases.canonical_answer: Prostate adenocarcinoma, Grade Group 5, with pleomorphic giant cell features
choices_raw: C. High grade papillary urothelial carcinoma
D. Prostate adenocarcinoma, Grade Group 5, with pleomorphic giant cell features
choices: Prostate adenocarcinoma, Grade Group 5, with pleomorphic giant cell features
cases.feedback_text: Sections show a high-grade cellular neoplasm with prominent nucleoli and papillary architecture. Paraganglioma can have abundant vascularity and marked nuclear atypia, but would typically show architecture that is more nested than papillary. Paragangliomas should lack keratin expression and would show labeling for neuroendocrine markers such as synaptophysin. Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma should have a high proliferation rate, often with basaloid nests with peripheral palisading. In the GU tract, this lesion should, by definition, lack any significant expression of prostate markers such as NKX3.1, PSA, or p501s, and should have significant expression of neuroendocrine markers. High grade papillary urothelial carcinoma can be difficult to distinguish from high grade prostatic adenocarcinoma invading the bladder, as both can show substantial papillary architecture. Marked nuclear pleomorphism, squamous differentiation, and an unequivocal precursor in-situ or non-invasive papillary urothelial neoplasm favor urothelial carcinoma. However, a low threshold for immunohistochemical confirmation is prudent given the substantial morphologic overlap. NKX3.1, p501s, and PSA expression indicate prostatic adenocarcinoma, whereas GATA3, uroplakin, and P63 are frequently expressed in urothelial carcinoma. Rare variants of prostatic adenocarcinoma in particular can mimic urothelial carcinoma. Adenosquamous carcinoma of the prostate can show bona fide squamous differentiation, and prostatic adenocarcinoma with pleomorphic giant cell features can show marked nuclear anaplasia, both leading to potential confusion with urothelial carcinoma. This patient had known recurrent prostatic adenocarcinoma causing urinary obstruction and bladder invasion. Despite the marked nuclear atypia and extensive papillary architecture, this tumor labeled diffusely with NKX3.1, confirming the diagnosis of prostatic adenocarcinoma with pleomorphic giant cell features.

cases.title: Week 775: Case 1

cases.vignette: This case is an elderly male who underwent a hydrocelectomy.
cases.question_text:
Cases presented by Dr. Ezra Baraban and prepared by Dr. Katherine Fomchenko.
This case is an elderly male who underwent a hydrocelectomy.
cases.feedback_text: Sections show benign mesothelial lined fibrous tissue consistent with a hydrocele sac. Scattered cellular clusters of crushed small round blue cells are also seen. The cellularity of these clusters raises concern for a neoplasm, as in a different context such as a transbronchial lung biopsy these foci would be concerning for a neuroendocrine neoplasm. In the setting of a hydrocele sac however, these clusters show the typical morphologic features of crushed aggregates of benign rete testis epithelium, which have shed into the hydrocele sac. Closer inspection reveals no mitotic activity and if performed, a Ki67 stain would be negligible, excluding any sort of neuroendocrine carcinoma, although keratin and CD56 labeling may be misleading if performed. Mesothelial markers would be negative in these cells, excluding the latter two diagnoses.

cases.vignette: This case is an elderly male presenting with a nasal mass.
cases.question_text:
Cases presented by Dr. Lisa Rooper and prepared by Dr. Katherine Fomchenko.
This case is an elderly male presenting with a nasal mass.
cases.histology: The lesion consists of a disorganized proliferation of normal elements predominantly composed of ciliated respiratory epithelium with scattered intermixed seromucinous glands. The stroma is variably edematous with scattered chronic inflammation and central areas of bone. All components of the lesion are cytologically benign.
cases.discussion:
The three most common sinonasal hamartomas are respiratory epithelial adenomatoid hamartoma (REAH), seromucinous hamartoma, and chondro-osseous respiratory epithelial (CORE) hamartoma. These hamartomas exist on a spectrum of morphologic components, with REAH having predominantly respiratory surface epithelium, seromucinous hamartomas having predominantly seromucinous glands, and CORE hamartomas having respiratory epithelium, seromucinous glands, bone, and cartilage. The etiology of these lesions is not fully understood. Another type of sinonasal hamartoma, chondromesenchymal hamartoma, is actually a neoplastic entity is driven by DICER1 mutations and is comprised of a range of immature to mature mesenchymal tissue and cartilage.

The lesion in this case exhibits remnants of an inverted sinonasal papilloma with transformation to a squamous cell carcinoma, and the identification of both components is key to the diagnosis. cases.question_text:
Cases presented by Dr. Lisa Rooper and prepared by Dr. Katherine Fomchenko.
This case is an older male presenting with a tonsil mass.
cases.histology: The lesion is composed of nests to sheets of large, atypical cells with markedly pleomorphic nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and scattered atypical mitoses that show a combination of pushing and infiltrative growth through background lymphocytes. There are scattered glandular spaces filled with cellular debris lined by atypical columnar cells, some of which are ciliated.
cases.discussion:
HPV- associated squamous cell carcinoma generally has a non-keratinizing morphology, with tumor cells that have large nuclei, scant eosinophilic cytoplasm, and minimal keratinization. These carcinomas have several histologic variants, including keratinizing, basaloid, sarcomatoid, lymphoepithelial, and adenosquamous. The adenosquamous variant shows a mix of squamous and glandular morphologies that can rarely be ciliated, as can be seen in this case. Cilia formation can complicate differentiating the tumor from benign upper aerodigestive lesions but the ciliated cells are closely intermixed with the tumor cells and are positive for p16 and high-risk HPV RNA in-situ hybridization. In general, histologic variants of HPV-associated squamous cell carcinoma do not affect prognosis, which is more favorable than HPV-negative squamous cell carcinomas of the head and neck.

The College of American Pathologists guidelines recommend that all new squamous cell carcinomas arising in the oropharynx or neck metastasis of unknown primary should be tested for involvement by high-risk HPV via p16 immunohistochemistry. In squamous cell carcinoma of the oropharynx and levels II and III of the neck, p16 positivity is regarded as diagnostic of HPV positivity due to the high pretest probability for HPV involvement. Outside of these sites, however, HPV specific testing such as in-situ hybridization or PCR is required to confirm involvement by HPV due to the imperfect specificity for p16 in non-oropharyngeal sites.

Bishop JA, Westra WH. Ciliated HPV-related Carcinoma: A Well-differentiated Form of Head and Neck Carcinoma That Can Be Mistaken for a Benign Cyst. Am J Surg Pathol. 2015 Nov;39(11):1591-5. doi: 10.1097/PAS.0000000000000521. PMID: 26457358; PMCID: PMC4602404.

cases.vignette: This case is an adult male with a bone lesion.
cases.question_text:
Cases presented by Dr. Marissa White and prepared by Dr. Katherine Fomchenko.
This case is an adult male with a bone lesion.
cases.histology: The lesion is composed of syncytial sheets of histiocytes with foamy to granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and background chronic inflammation. Focal basophilic round to targetoid appearing cytoplasmic inclusions are scattered throughout.
cases.discussion:
Malakoplakia is a rare, benign, mass-like lesion usually seen in the genitourinary tract and is associated with infection. It is composed of sheets of distinctive histocytes with eosinophilic granular cytoplasm called von Hansemann cells with interspersed acute and chronic inflammatory cells. The histiocytes also have basophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions called Michaelis-Gutmann bodies, which are a distinct diagnostic feature. These will stain positive for calcium. Malakoplakia of the bone is exceedingly rare, and some case reports have noted an association with osteomyelitis.

Lane JL, Land AD, Thompson SM, Weiner SD. Malakoplakia of Bone: A Case Report and Review of the Literature. JBJS Case Connect. 2014 Oct/Dec/Nov;4(4):e116. doi: 10.2106/JBJS.CC.N.00103. PMID: 29252784.

cases.title: Week 773: Case 2
cases.attribution: Cases presented by Dr. Marissa White and prepared by Dr. Katherine Fomchenko.
cases.vignette: This case is an adult female with a lung mass.
cases.question_text:
Cases presented by Dr. Marissa White and prepared by Dr. Katherine Fomchenko.
This case is an adult female with a lung mass.
cases.histology: This lesion is composed of large cells with round, basophilic nuclei with focal nuclear molding and small nucleoli growing in a sheet-like to nested architecture with an infiltrative growth pattern, focal necrosis, and a high mitotic rate. The cytoplasm is not overwhelmingly abundant. On immunostains (not shown), the neoplastic cells were positive for chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and TTF-1.
cases.discussion:
Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma is an aggressive, high grade carcinoid tumor comprised of large polygonal cells growing in an organoid pattern. The four types of neuroendocrine tumors of the lung are typical carcinoid tumor, atypical carcinoid tumor, large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma, and small cell lung carcinoma. Typical and atypical carcinoid tumors are low grade lesions showing low amounts of proliferation (2 mitoses per 10 HPF for typical carcinoid, 2-10 per 10 HPF for atypical carcinoid) and mild nuclear atypia. Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma and small cell lung carcinoma are high grade lesions with significant proliferation (>11 mitoses per 10 HPF) and atypia and are composed of large and small cells, respectively. All of these lesions will have some neuroendocrine differentiation, but it may be lower in higher grade lesions. Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma and small cell lung carcinoma are also TTF-1 positive. In this case, the cells are not as large as expected and appear somewhat monotonous, lacking the vesicular chromatin usually present. Though it presents with a more typical carcinoid morphology, the mitotic rate and necrosis indicate a higher rate of proliferation, placing this lesion into the large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma category despite appearing closer to an atypical carcinoid.

Gollard R, Jhatakia S, Elliott M, Kosty M. Large cell/neuroendocrine carcinoma. Lung Cancer. 2010 Jul;69(1):13-8. doi: 10.1016/j.lungcan.2009.12.011. Epub 2010 Feb 4. PMID: 20133008.
Rekhtman N. Lung neuroendocrine neoplasms: recent progress and persistent challenges. Mod Pathol. 2022 Jan;35(Suppl 1):36-50. doi: 10.1038/s41379-021-00943-2. Epub 2021 Oct 18. PMID: 34663914; PMCID: PMC8695375.
